lessons.title: What is Home-Based Catering?
lessons.body: Home-based catering means preparing food in your own kitchen and delivering it to clients for small events like birthdays, weddings, or corporate lunches. You are not running a restaurant; you cook in bulk at home, then transport the food to the event venue or deliver it ready to serve. In Africa, this model works well because you avoid high rent for a commercial space. You can start with one gas cooker, a few large pots, and a reliable motorbike or car for delivery. For example, in Nairobi, a home caterer might prepare 50 plates of pilau and kachumbari for a graduation party, charging KES 500 per plate. Your profit comes from your cooking skill, your ability to buy ingredients in bulk, and your reputation for punctuality. You must be organized: take orders at least 3 days in advance, shop the day before, and cook early on the event day. Unlike a restaurant, you don't need a dining area, but you do need a clean kitchen, safe food handling, and a way to keep food hot or cold during transport. Start small: offer a set menu for 20â30 people. As you gain trust, you can expand to 100 plates or more. Remember, your home is your production site, so keep it clean, pest-free, and separate from family living areas as much as possible. This business is low-cost to start but demands discipline and consistency.

lessons.title: Legal Requirements and Permits
lessons.body: Before you sell your first plate, you need to know the legal rules for home-based food businesses in your country. In most African countries, you must register your business with the local government or companies office. For example, in Kenya, you register with the Business Registration Service and get a business permit from your county. In Nigeria, you register with the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC) and obtain a food handler's certificate from the local government. In South Africa, you need a Certificate of Acceptability from your municipality. These permits ensure your kitchen meets basic hygiene standards. You will also need a food handler's medical certificate, which requires a stool test and typhoid vaccination. This costs about $20â$50 and must be renewed yearly. If you deliver food, you may need a food transport permit. For home-based catering, many countries allow you to operate from home if you have a separate kitchen area and proper waste disposal. You must also pay taxes on your income. Keep records of all sales and expenses. Some local councils require an inspection of your kitchen before issuing a permit. The inspector will check for clean water, handwashing facilities, pest control, and proper refrigeration. Do not skip these steps: operating illegally can lead to fines or closure. Start by visiting your local health department or business office to ask for a checklist. It may take 2â4 weeks and cost $100â$300 total, but it protects your business and builds client trust.

lessons.title: Assessing Your Home Kitchen
lessons.body: Your home kitchen must be able to handle bulk cooking without compromising safety. First, measure your workspace: you need at least 2 meters of clear counter space for chopping and plating. Check your water source: you need running water, preferably treated or boiled, for washing hands and utensils. If you only have a shared tap, plan to store water in clean jerrycans. Next, look at your cooking capacity. A single-burner gas cooker can handle one large pot, but for 50 plates you need at least two burners or a large charcoal stove. Count your pots: you need at least one 20-liter pot for rice or stew, one 10-liter pot for vegetables, and a large frying pan. Refrigeration is critical: you need a fridge that can hold 20â30 kg of meat or vegetables at 4Â°C or below. If you don't have a fridge, you must buy fresh ingredients daily and cook immediately. Check your storage: you need airtight containers for dry goods like rice, flour, and spices. Your kitchen must have a handwashing station with soap and a towel. Pest control is non-negotiable: seal cracks, use screens on windows, and store food off the floor. Also, consider your family: if you share the kitchen, schedule your cooking times so you don't cross-contaminate. Finally, think about ventilation: a window or exhaust fan to remove smoke and heat. If your kitchen fails any of these, fix it before you take orders. A simple upgrade like adding a second burner or a plastic table for prep can make a big difference.

lessons.title: Essential Equipment for Small Events
lessons.body: To cater for 20â50 people, you need specific tools that can handle volume. Start with cooking equipment: two large gas cookers (or one gas and one charcoal stove), at least three 20-liter pots, two 10-liter pots, and a large frying pan. You also need a heavy-duty knife set, a chopping board (separate ones for meat and vegetables), and a large wooden spoon or spatula. For measuring, get a kitchen scale (up to 5 kg) and measuring cups. For food safety, you need a thermometer to check meat doneness (75Â°C for chicken) and a fridge thermometer. For transport, invest in insulated food carriers or coolers. In Africa, you can buy large plastic coolers (like the 50-liter Igloo) for about $40. You also need chafing dishes or hot boxes to keep food warm. A simple alternative is a large pot wrapped in a blanket inside a cardboard box. For serving, get disposable plates, cutlery, and napkins in bulk. You'll need serving spoons, tongs, and gloves. For cleaning, have plenty of dish soap, sponges, and bleach. Don't forget a first aid kit and fire extinguisher. If you deliver, you need a motorbike or car with a clean, covered carrier. A hand truck helps move heavy pots. Buy equipment gradually: start with the basics (pots, knives, cooler) and add as you earn. Many items can be found second-hand in local markets. Keep a list and prioritize safety and capacity over brand names.

lessons.title: Setting Up a Workflow
lessons.body: A good workflow prevents chaos and keeps food safe. Start by planning your menu and shopping list 3 days before the event. The day before, shop for all ingredients, then wash and chop vegetables, marinate meat, and cook any sauces that can be reheated. Store everything in the fridge in labeled containers. On event day, wake up early and follow a timed schedule. For example: 6:00 AM start cooking rice; 7:00 AM cook stew; 8:00 AM fry plantains; 9:00 AM pack food into insulated carriers. Work in zones: a prep zone (chopping), a cooking zone (stoves), and a packing zone (coolers). Keep raw and cooked food separate. Use color-coded chopping boards (red for meat, green for vegetables). Clean as you go: wash dishes immediately to avoid pests. Assign tasks if you have help: one person chops, one cooks, one packs. For delivery, load food last, keep hot food above 60Â°C and cold food below 5Â°C. At the venue, set up a serving station with gloves, tongs, and trash bags. After the event, collect leftovers, clean equipment, and record what worked and what didn't. A written checklist for each event helps you improve. Time yourself: if you promise food at noon, start cooking at 6 AM. Always add a 30-minute buffer for transport delays. With practice, you can cater for 50 people in 4 hours. Without a workflow, you risk late food, cold food, or food poisoning.

lessons.title: Basic Food Safety Certification
lessons.body: Food safety certification proves you know how to handle food without making people sick. In most African countries, you need a Food Handler's Certificate from your local health authority. The training covers four key areas: personal hygiene, temperature control, cross-contamination, and cleaning. For personal hygiene, you must wash hands for 20 seconds with soap before cooking, after using the toilet, and after handling raw meat. Wear clean aprons and tie back hair. If you are sick, do not cook. For temperature control, keep hot food above 60Â°C and cold food below 5Â°C. Cook chicken to 75Â°C, beef to 63Â°C, and reheat leftovers to 74Â°C. Use a thermometer, not guesswork. For cross-contamination, use separate cutting boards and knives for raw meat and vegetables. Never put cooked food on a plate that held raw meat. Store raw meat on the bottom shelf of the fridge. For cleaning, sanitize surfaces with a bleach solution (1 tablespoon bleach per 4 liters water). Wash dishes in hot soapy water, then air dry. The certification course usually takes 1 day and costs $10â$30. You will take a short written test. After passing, you get a card valid for 1â2 years. Some countries require renewals with a new stool test. Display your certificate at your kitchen or include it in your client proposals. It shows you are professional and reduces your legal risk. Even if not required, take the course: it prevents foodborne illness, which can destroy your reputation.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of home-based catering over a restaurant?
options: A) You can serve more customers
B) You avoid high rent for commercial space
C) You don't need any permits
D) You can cook without a license
quiz.explanation: Home-based catering uses your own kitchen, so you save on rent for a commercial space.

quiz.q: In the example, how much does a home caterer in Nairobi charge per plate of pilau?
quiz.explanation: The lesson states a home caterer might charge KES 500 per plate.

quiz.q: How many days in advance should you take orders for a small event?
quiz.explanation: The lesson recommends taking orders at least 3 days in advance.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a typical legal requirement for home-based catering?
quiz.explanation: A commercial kitchen license is for restaurants, not home-based caterers.

quiz.q: In Kenya, where do you register your business?
quiz.explanation: The lesson says in Kenya you register with the Business Registration Service.

quiz.q: What does a food handler's medical certificate require?
options: B) A stool test and typhoid vaccination
quiz.explanation: The lesson states it requires a stool test and typhoid vaccination.

quiz.q: How much does a food handler's certificate typically cost?
quiz.explanation: The lesson says it costs about $20â$50 and must be renewed yearly.

quiz.q: What is the minimum clear counter space recommended for a home catering kitchen?
quiz.explanation: The lesson says you need at least 2 meters of clear counter space.

quiz.q: At what temperature should your fridge hold meat or vegetables?
quiz.explanation: The lesson states 4Â°C or below for safe refrigeration.

quiz.q: If you don't have a fridge, what should you do?
options: A) Buy fresh ingredients daily and cook immediately
B) Keep food in a cool box with ice
quiz.explanation: The lesson says if you don't have a fridge, buy fresh ingredients daily and cook immediately.

quiz.q: Why is pest control critical in a home catering kitchen?
options: C) To keep the kitchen looking clean
quiz.explanation: Pests can contaminate food and cause illness.

quiz.q: How many large pots (20-liter) are recommended for catering 20â50 people?
quiz.explanation: The lesson says at least three 20-liter pots.

quiz.q: What internal temperature should chicken reach to be safe?
quiz.explanation: The lesson states chicken must be cooked to 75Â°C.

quiz.q: What is a cheaper alternative to a chafing dish for keeping food warm?
options: B) A pot wrapped in a blanket inside a cardboard box
quiz.explanation: The lesson suggests wrapping a pot in a blanket inside a cardboard box.

quiz.q: Why should you have separate chopping boards for meat and vegetables?
quiz.explanation: Separate boards prevent cross-contamination between raw meat and vegetables.

quiz.q: When should you start cooking on the event day if you promise food at noon?
quiz.explanation: The lesson says start cooking at 6 AM for a noon delivery, with a 30-minute buffer.

quiz.q: What is a good practice for cleaning as you go?
options: B) Leave dishes until the end
quiz.explanation: Washing dishes immediately prevents pests and keeps the workspace clean.

quiz.q: How long should you wash your hands with soap?
quiz.explanation: The lesson says wash hands for 20 seconds with soap.

quiz.q: What is the safe minimum temperature for holding hot food?
quiz.explanation: Hot food must be kept above 60Â°C.

quiz.q: What should you do if you are sick?
options: A) Wear a mask and cook
quiz.explanation: The lesson says if you are sick, do not cook to avoid contaminating food.

quiz.q: How do you sanitize surfaces with bleach?
options: A) 1 tablespoon bleach per 4 liters water
B) 1 cup bleach per 1 liter water
C) 1 teaspoon bleach per 1 liter water
quiz.explanation: The lesson specifies 1 tablespoon bleach per 4 liters of water.

quiz.q: How long does a food handler's certificate usually last?
quiz.explanation: The lesson says the card is valid for 1â2 years.

quiz.q: Why should you display your food safety certificate?
options: B) To build client trust and reduce legal risk
quiz.explanation: Displaying it shows professionalism and builds trust.

quiz.q: What is the first step in setting up a workflow?
options: B) Plan menu and shopping list 3 days before
quiz.explanation: The lesson says start by planning your menu and shopping list 3 days before.

quiz.q: What should you do the day before an event?
options: B) Shop, wash, chop, and marinate
quiz.explanation: The day before, shop and do prep like washing, chopping, and marinating.

quiz.q: What is a prep zone?
options: B) Where you chop and prepare ingredients
quiz.explanation: The prep zone is for chopping and preparing ingredients.

quiz.q: How can you keep hot food above 60Â°C during transport?
options: C) Put in a plastic bag
quiz.explanation: Insulated food carriers help maintain hot temperatures.

quiz.q: What should you do after an event?
options: B) Collect leftovers, clean, and record what worked
quiz.explanation: The lesson says collect leftovers, clean equipment, and record lessons learned.

quiz.q: How many people can you cater for in 4 hours with a good workflow?
quiz.explanation: The lesson says with practice, you can cater for 50 people in 4 hours.

quiz.q: What is the recommended internal temperature for reheating leftovers?
quiz.explanation: The lesson states reheat leftovers to 74Â°C.
